newsitem.title: KENYA: Calm returns after nine killed in Kenyan unrest.
newsitem.headline: Calm returns after nine killed in Kenyan unrest.

text.p: Kenyan cities and towns were calm on Tuesday, a day after at least nine people were killed in the country's most violent clashes between protesters and police in seven years.
Security remained tight in the capital Nairobi after opposition groups vowed to resume protests to push for constitutional reforms.

The National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), made up of opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies, on Monday night ordered new demonstrations for Wednesday to put pressure on the government.
The NCEC called for three days of national mourning from Wednesday to Friday "for the gallant sons and daughters who were killed by the government during the Saba Saba commemoration".
But police expected the latest opposition call to go unheeded.

"I don't think that Kenyans will heed that call. What Kenyans are saying is that all avenues open for change have not been exploited. Why should people turn to violence," said police spokesman Assistant Commissioner Peter Kimanthi.
Kimanthi said that at least nine people were killed in the violence on Monday but calm had returned.
Four people died in the Rift Valley town of Nyahururu, two died in Nairobi and one in Thika after protests called to commemorate "Saba Saba" turned violent.

A minibus driver speeding away from riots killed a seven-year-old girl in the Kawangware shantytown of Nairobi and the minibus driver was lynched to death by residents, Kimanthi said, adding that police were investigating the incidents.
"Saba Saba" is a Kiswahili word that refers to July 7, 1990, when at least 20 people died after a rally in Nairobi to press for a switch to pluralist politics was dispersed by police.
Nairobi University students, who blocked the main Uhuru highway through the capital for hours late on Monday, were back in their campus where they are sitting semester examinations.
Kenyan newspapers splashed the events of "Saba Saba" on their front pages. The East African Standard trumpeted the "Horror of Saba Saba" and "National day of shame and disgrace".
Kimanthi said a policeman shot in the stomach by a man firing from a crowd was "stable and out of danger".
He said police were investigating reports that a policeman had shot dead a man in the Kawangware area on Monday.

The NCEC said Kenyans on Wednesday would "demonstrate their displeasure" with the government hosting a summit on Sudan's civil war under the six-nation Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD) in Nairobi during the mourning period.
Regional presidents were arriving in Kenya on Monday and early on Tuesday for the summit to start later on Wednesday.
"Our position and demand of the IGAD meeting is no reforms, no IGAD meeting," the NCEC said in a statement. Police said they would block any demonstrators who failed to apply for a permit.
"The campaign for civil disobedience must continue if no tangible actions are seen towards reforms. Towns will be closed down many times in the future," said Koigi wa Wamwere, a leading dissident.

Joseph Kamotho, secretary-general of President Daniel arap Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union party, condemned Monday's violence as part of a plot to hijack democracy, block the impending general election and seize power by force.
The NCEC says the law requiring a permit for demonstrations is itself unconstitutional and therefore is null and void.
Moi, 73, is almost certain to win another five-year term from this year's presidential and parliamentary elections, for which no dates have been set, because the opposition is split.
